name: Cuba
summary_text: Private, non-commercial sexual relations between consenting same-sex adults aged 16 and over have been lawful in Cuba since 1979, when the Social Defence Code that treated homosexual practices as a social threat was repealed. The offence of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987. The offence of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was amended in 1997 to refer only to sexual requests.  Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. It was the first constitutional text to name both grounds expressly. The definition of marriage as between a man and a woman in Article 36 was removed in the February 2019 referendum, with marriage defined on the basis of free will and equality of rights.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is unlawful in Cuba. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is also unlawful. In employment, Law 116 and the labour amendment approved in December 2013 bar discrimination on sexual orientation. Article 2(b) of the Labour Code covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground.  Following the Family Code referendum on 25 September 2022, Cuba recognises same-sex marriage and unions, same-sex adoption and non-commercial surrogacy. The referendum proposal also included codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. The Code confirms that legal gender change does not require surgery.  Transgender health care is provided within the public health system under Resolution 126 of 2008.  Police received orders in 1988 not to harass lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons after repeal of the 1938 Public Ostentation Law. In 2001 police prevented gay and trans persons from meeting in the street, fined them and closed meeting places. In 2004 police conducted a campaign directed at travestis and arrested persons dressed in women's clothing.  Since 1993 lesbian, gay and bisexual persons and transgender persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces.  Pride parades are held in Havana every May to coincide with the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing each year. Cuba voted in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025 in favour of renewing the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

sources.documents: BBC documents police campaign specifically against travestis/transvestites for cross-dressing; Miami Herald documents 2019 state cancellation of anti-homophobia march and arrest of 3 independent marchers.

name: Curaçao
summary_text: Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It holds full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.  Same-sex sexual activity, both male and female, is legal in Curaçao. The age of consent is 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.  Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upholding the Appeals Court decision that barring such marriages discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation.  Before that ruling, Curaçao was required as part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to recognise as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. Same-sex couples could not marry in Curaçao itself and no civil unions or other forms of recognition were available.  The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation". Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference which has the purpose or effect of impacting or affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties including fines and imprisonment of up to one year.  The European Court of Human Rights has jurisdiction over Curaçao. In Oliari and Others v. Italy in August 2015 it held that providing no legal recognition to same-sex couples is discriminatory.  In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that lesbian, gay and bisexual people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement records a political commitment to equal treatment. It does not create an immediately enforceable right that a visitor can invoke at a border or in a local court.  Curaçao Commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in April 2015. Her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed that position and had forced the 2013 Curaçao Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel through a last-minute exceptionally strict permit requirement.  Curaçao opened an LGBT Pink House centre in 2010. Curaçao Gay Pride representative Frank Holtslag has cited the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association award describing Curaçao as most gay welcoming in the region.
